brief.situation: 10:00 in labor and delivery. You are the RN. Ms. Rivera, 28, first baby, 39 weeks, is being induced with oxytocin; the rate was increased per protocol 30 minutes ago. She is 5 cm, semi-sitting, comfortable with an epidural. The central monitor flags her tracing.
handover: Tracing at 09:00: baseline 140, moderate variability, accelerations. Now you see contractions coming close together.
Oxytocin protocol: titrate to adequate labor; stop the infusion for tachysystole or an abnormal tracing and notify the obstetrician. Terbutaline only on the obstetrician's order.
IV lactated Ringer's at maintenance; a bolus is allowed by protocol for hypotension or intrauterine resuscitation.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
The tracing changes over minutes, not seconds; contractions take a while to space out after oxytocin stops.
Partway through you are asked to write how you read the tracing. The case ends at 10:45, then a debrief scores what you did.

why.question: How do you read Ms. Rivera's tracing, and what do you do first?

parts.label: Interpretation
parts.criteria: Names tachysystole (more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes over 30) with recurrent late decelerations and falling variability; contrasts it with the reassuring pattern (baseline 110-160, moderate variability).
parts.modelAnswer: Tachysystole, six in ten, with a late deceleration after each contraction and variability drifting down: uteroplacental insufficiency from too much uterine activity. A reassuring tracing would be 110 to 160 with moderate variability.

parts.label: First actions
parts.criteria: Stops the oxytocin and turns her to her side first; bolus; SBAR to the obstetrician with the numbers; terbutaline only on order; does not lay her flat or increase the oxytocin.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the oxytocin and turn her to her left side, then a bolus and an SBAR to the obstetrician with the numbers. Terbutaline when ordered. Never flat on her back and never more oxytocin.

expertPath.text: Read the strip: six contractions in ten, late decelerations, variability falling. Tachysystole, Category II.
Stop the oxytocin. Turn her to her left side. Bolus.
SBAR to the obstetrician with the numbers; terbutaline when ordered.
Contractions spaced, variability moderate, lates gone. Restart only on the obstetrician's plan.

emergencyBirth.headline: A prolonged deceleration
emergencyBirth.body: Tachysystole with late decelerations is fixed at its cause: stop the oxytocin and turn her to her side, first. Increasing it, halving it or laying her flat let the fetus run out of reserve.

resolvedFast.headline: Tracing back to reassuring
resolvedFast.body: You read the tracing, stopped the oxytocin, turned her to her side, gave a bolus and the terbutaline, and told the obstetrician in numbers. That is the expert path.

resolvedLate.headline: Resolved, by a slower route
resolvedLate.body: Check how soon the oxytocin stopped (not halved), when she was turned, whether she was ever flat, and whether the obstetrician heard numbers.

time_up.headline: Still abnormal
time_up.body: Stop the oxytocin and reposition first.

scoring.modelReasoning: More than five contractions in ten minutes averaged over thirty is tachysystole, and a late deceleration after each contraction with falling variability says the placenta cannot keep up. A reassuring tracing is a baseline of 110 to 160 with moderate variability (6-25 bpm). The first responses are at the cause: stop the oxytocin and turn her to her left side, add a fluid bolus, and tell the obstetrician the baseline, variability, decelerations and contraction count; terbutaline is given on the obstetrician's order. Laying her flat drops her blood pressure and placental flow, and more oxytocin makes it worse.
